dhpak1.13:1.1: 1.12 The Story about Devadatta Devadattassa Vatthu
dhpak1.13:2.1: “Here he suffers, after death he suffers,” {1.133} this Dhamma teaching was given by the Teacher while in residence at
dhpak1.13:3.1: The story of Devadatta, from the time he went forth to the time the earth opened and swallowed him up, is related in detail
dhpak1.13:3.2: in all the Birth Stories. The following is a synopsis of the story:
dhpak1.13:5.1: While the Teacher was in residence at Anupiya Mango Grove, which lies near Anupiya, a market-town of the Mallas,
dhpak1.13:5.2: 80,000 [28.231] kinsmen one day recognized on him the characteristics of a Realised One, and 80,000 relatives asserted:
dhpak1.13:5.3: “Let him be a king or a Buddha, he will spend his days surrounded by a retinue of nobles.” After all but six of these
dhpak1.13:5.4: youths had gone forth and become bhikkhus, the company of princes, observing that the six Sakyan princes, King Bhaddiya,
dhpak1.13:5.5: Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimbila, and Devadatta, had not yet gone forth, discussed the matter as follows:
dhpak1.13:5.6: “We let only our own sons go forth. But of course these six Sakyan princes are not kinsmen of the Buddha. For this reason,
dhpak1.13:5.7: doubtless, they have not gone forth.” Now one day the Sakyan prince Mahānāma approached Anuruddha and said: “Friend,
dhpak1.13:5.8: there isn’t one of our family who has gone forth. You go forth and I will follow your example.”
dhpak1.13:6.1: Now Anuruddha is said to have been brought up in such softness and luxury that he had never heard the words No More (Natthi) before.
dhpak1.13:6.2: For example, one day these six Sakyan princes engaged in a game of marbles. Anuruddha staked cakes on the result,
dhpak1.13:6.3: proved a loser, and sent home for cakes. His mother prepared cakes and sent them. {1.134} The princes ate the cakes and resumed their play.
dhpak1.13:7.1: Anuruddha lost repeatedly. Three times in all his mother sent him cakes. The fourth time she sent back word:
dhpak1.13:7.2: “There is no more cake to send. Now Anuruddha had never before heard the words No More. Therefore, supposing that this
dhpak1.13:7.3: must be a variety of cake, he sent the man back, saying to him: “Fetch me some No More cakes.” When his mother received the message:
dhpak1.13:7.4: “Then, my lady, send me some No More cakes,” she thought to herself: “My son has never heard the words No More before.
dhpak1.13:7.5: By this means, however, I can teach him the meaning of it.” So she took an empty golden bowl, covered it with another golden bowl,
dhpak1.13:7.6: and sent it to her son.
dhpak1.13:8.1: The guardian Devatās of the city thought: “When Anuruddha the Sakyan was Annabhāra, he gave food that was his own portion
dhpak1.13:8.2: to the Paccekabuddha Upariṭṭha, making the aspiration: ‘May I never hear the words No More; may I never know where food comes from.’
dhpak1.13:8.3: Now if he sees the empty bowl, we shall never be able to enter the assembly of the Devas; it may even happen that our
dhpak1.13:8.4: heads will split into seven pieces.” So they filled the bowl with celestial cakes. As soon as the bowl was set down on
dhpak1.13:8.5: the round platter uncovered, the fragrance of the cakes permeated the entire city. Moreover, the moment a morsel of cake
dhpak1.13:8.6: was placed in the mouth, it thrilled the seven thousand nerves of taste.
dhpak1.13:9.1: Anuruddha thought to himself: “My mother does not love me; all this time she has never fried this No More cake [28.232] for me.
dhpak1.13:9.2: {1.135} From this time forth I shall eat no other kind of cake.” So he went home and asked his mother: “Mother,
dhpak1.13:9.3: do you love me or do you not?” – “My dear son, even as the eye is dear to one who possesses but one eye, and even as the heart,
dhpak1.13:9.4: so are you exceedingly dear to me.” – “Then, dear mother, why is it that all this time you have not fried No More cake for me?”
dhpak1.13:9.5: Said the mother to her little prince: “Boy, is there nothing in the bowl?” – “My lady, the plate is filled to overflowing with cakes,
dhpak1.13:9.6: and with such cakes as I have never seen before.”
dhpak1.13:10.1: The mother thought to herself: “It must be that my son has acquired great merit; it must be that he has made an aspiration;
dhpak1.13:10.2: Devatās must have filled the plate with cakes and sent them.” Said the son to the mother: “Dear mother, from this time
dhpak1.13:10.3: forth I will eat no other kind of cake than this; henceforth, I pray you, fry No More cake alone for me.” From that time forth,
dhpak1.13:10.4: whenever her son said: “I should like some cakes to eat,” she would send a bowl absolutely empty, covered with another bowl.
dhpak1.13:10.5: So long as he continued to live at home, during all that time Devatās sent him celestial cakes. Since Anuruddha was so
dhpak1.13:10.6: unsophisticated as all this, how could he be expected to know the meaning of the expression going forth?
dhpak1.13:11.1: For this reason, therefore, he asked his brother: “What is this going forth?” His brother replied: “Going forth involves
dhpak1.13:11.2: cutting off the hair and beard, sleeping with indifference whether in a thorn-brake or in a fine bed, and going the rounds for alms,”
dhpak1.13:11.3: Anuruddha replied: “Friend, I am exceedingly delicate; I shall never be able {1.136} to go forth.” – “Very well,
dhpak1.13:11.4: my dear brother, then learn farming and live the life of a householder. But at least one of us must go forth.”
dhpak1.13:11.5: Then said Anuruddha: “What is this farming?”
dhpak1.13:12.1: How could you expect a youth to know the meaning of the word farming who did not know where food comes from? For example,
dhpak1.13:12.2: on a certain day a discussion arose among the three princes Kimbila, Bhaddiya, and Anuruddha as to where food comes from.
dhpak1.13:12.3: Kimbila said: “It comes from the barn.” Bhaddiya said to him: “You do not know where food comes from; it comes from a pot.”
dhpak1.13:12.4: Anuruddha said: “Both of you together do not know where food comes from. It comes from a golden bowl with a jeweled knob.”
dhpak1.13:13.1: We are told that one day Kimbila saw rice being removed from a barn, and immediately formed the opinion:
dhpak1.13:13.2: “These grains of rice were produced in the barn.” Likewise one day Bhaddiya saw food being taken out of a pot, and formed the opinion:
dhpak1.13:13.3: “It was produced [28.233] in a pot.” Anuruddha, however, had never seen men pounding rice or boiling it or taking it out of a pot,
dhpak1.13:13.4: but had seen it only after it had been taken out of a pot and set before him. So Anuruddha formed the opinion:
dhpak1.13:13.5: “When one desires to eat, food makes its appearance in a golden bowl.” Such was the ignorance of all three princes as to
dhpak1.13:14.1: Now when Anuruddha asked the question: “What is this farming?” he received the following answer: “First the field must be plowed,
dhpak1.13:14.2: and after that such and such other things must be done, and these things must be done year after year.” He said to himself:
dhpak1.13:14.3: “When will the duties connected with farming ever come to an end? When shall we ever have time to enjoy our possessions in peace?”
dhpak1.13:14.4: And because it seemed to him that the duties connected with farming would never come to an end and never cease,
dhpak1.13:14.5: he said to his brother: “Well then, if this is the case, you may live the life of a householder. But as for me, I have no use for it.”
dhpak1.13:14.6: Accordingly he approached his mother {1.137} and said to her: “Mother, give me your permission; I wish to go forth.”
dhpak1.13:15.1: Thrice Anuruddha requested his mother to give him permission to go forth, and thrice she refused to do so. Finally she said to him:
dhpak1.13:15.2: “If your friend King Bhaddiya will go forth, then you may go forth with him.” Accordingly he approached his friend Bhaddiya and said to him:
dhpak1.13:15.3: “Friend, whether I shall go forth or not is conditional upon your going forth.” Anuruddha urged his friend Bhaddiya with
dhpak1.13:15.4: every argument at his command to go forth, and finally, on the seventh day, obtained Bhaddiya’s promise to go forth with him.
dhpak1.13:16.1: So six princes of the noble caste, Bhaddiya, King of the Sakyans, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimbila, and Devadatta,
dhpak1.13:16.2: accompanied by Upāli the barber as the seventh man, for seven days enjoyed celestial glory like gods, and then set out
dhpak1.13:16.3: with fourfold array, as though on their way to a pleasure-garden. When they reached foreign territory, they turned back
dhpak1.13:16.4: their army by royal command, and then entered foreign territory. There each of the six princes removed his own ornaments,
dhpak1.13:16.5: made a bundle of them, and gave them to Upāli, saying: “Now, Upāli, turn back. All this wealth will suffice to provide
dhpak1.13:16.6: you with a means of livelihood.” Upāli flung himself at their feet, rolled over and over on the ground, and wept bitterly.
dhpak1.13:16.7: But not daring to disobey the order, he arose and turned back. When they parted, the forest wept, as it were,
dhpak1.13:16.8: and the earth quaked, as it were.
dhpak1.13:17.1: When Upāli had gone a little way, he thought to himself: “Harsh and cruel are these Sakyans; they may kill me,
dhpak1.13:17.2: thinking I have killed their friends. These Sakyan princes have renounced all this splendor, have cast away these priceless
dhpak1.13:17.3: ornaments like a mass of saliva, and intend to go forth; {1.138} why not I?” So saying, he untied the bundle,
dhpak1.13:17.4: hung those ornaments on a tree, and said: “Let those who want them take them.” Having so done, he went to the Sakyan princes,
dhpak1.13:17.5: and when they asked him why he had turned back, told them the whole story.
dhpak1.13:18.1: So the six Sakyan princes took Upāli the barber with them, went to the Teacher, and said to him: “We, venerable Sir,
dhpak1.13:18.2: are proud Sakyans. This man has been a servitor of ours for a long time. Give him the going forth first;
dhpak1.13:18.3: to him first we will offer respectful salutations; so will our pride be humbled.” Thus first did they cause Upāli the
dhpak1.13:18.4: barber to go forth, and after that they went forth themselves.
dhpak1.13:19.1: Of the six Sakyan princes. Venerable Bhaddiya attained threefold knowledge in that very rainy season.
dhpak1.13:19.2: Venerable Anuruddha attained divine eye, and after listening to the Discourse entitled: “The Discourse on the Great Reflections,”
dhpak1.13:19.3: attained Arahatship. Venerable Ānanda was established in the fruition of Stream-entry. Elder Bhagu and Elder Kimbila
dhpak1.13:19.4: subsequently developed spiritual insight and attained Arahatship. Devadatta attained the lower grade of psychic power.
dhpak1.13:20.1: After a time, while the Teacher was in residence at Kosambī, rich gain and honor accrued to the Realised One and his company of disciples.
dhpak1.13:20.2: Men entered the monastery bearing in their hands robes, medicines, and other offerings and asked: “Where is the Teacher?
dhpak1.13:20.3: Where is the Elder Sāriputta? Where is the Elder Moggallāna? Where is the Elder Kassapa? Where is the Elder Bhaddiya?
dhpak1.13:20.4: Where is the Elder Anuruddha? Where is the Elder Ānanda? Where is the Elder Bhagu? Where is the Elder Kimbila?” So saying,
dhpak1.13:20.5: they went about looking at the places where the eighty Great Disciples sat.
dhpak1.13:22.1: Since no one asked: “Where does the Elder Devadatta sit and stand?” Devadatta thought to himself: “I went forth at the
dhpak1.13:22.2: same time as these other bhikkhus. Even as they are men of the noble caste who have gone forth, so also am I a man of the
dhpak1.13:22.3: noble caste who has gone forth. {1.139} But whereas men bearing rich [28.235] offerings seek out these bhikkhus,
dhpak1.13:22.4: no one takes my name on his lips. With whom now can I make common cause? With whom can I ingratiate myself so that I may
dhpak1.13:22.5: obtain gain and honor for myself?”
dhpak1.13:23.1: A Wicked Thought Then the following thought occurred to him: “This King Bimbisāra, on the day when he first saw the Buddha,
dhpak1.13:23.2: became established in the fruition of Stream-entry, together with 110,000 men besides; I cannot make common cause with him.
dhpak1.13:23.3: Neither can I make common cause with the king of Kosala. But this king’s son Ajātasattu knows no one’s good or bad qualities;
dhpak1.13:23.4: I will make common cause with him.”
dhpak1.13:24.1: Accordingly Devadatta departed from Kosambī to Rājagaha, transformed himself into a youth, put four snakes on his hands and feet,
dhpak1.13:24.2: put one snake about his neck, coiled one snake about his head as a cushion-rest, placed one snake on one shoulder,
dhpak1.13:24.3: and thus arrayed in a girdle of snakes, he descended from the air and seated himself in Ajātasattu’s lap.
dhpak1.13:24.4: Ajātasattu was frightened and said: “Who are you?” – “I am Devadatta.” In order to dispel Ajātasattu’s fear,
dhpak1.13:24.5: Devadatta changed his form, stood before Ajātasattu wearing the robe of a bhikkhu and carrying a bowl, ingratiated himself
dhpak1.13:24.6: with Ajātasattu, and obtained for himself gain and honor.
dhpak1.13:25.1: Overcome with the gain and honor he received, Devadatta thought to himself: “It is I who ought to be at the head of the
dhpak1.13:25.2: assembly of bhikkhus.” Once having allowed this wicked thought to spring up in his breast, with the springing up of the
dhpak1.13:25.3: wicked thought Devadatta lost the power to work miracles.
dhpak1.13:26.1: Now at this time the Teacher was teaching the Dhamma to the assembly at the Veḷuvana monastery, and the king was among the assembly.
dhpak1.13:26.2: While the Fortunate One was teaching the Dhamma, Devadatta worshipped him, and then rising from his seat,
dhpak1.13:26.3: extended his hands in an attitude of reverent salutation and said: “Venerable Sir, the Fortunate One is now worn out,
dhpak1.13:26.4: stricken with years, and aged; let him live a pleasant life in this world, free from care. I will direct the Saṅgha of bhikkhus;
dhpak1.13:26.5: commit the Saṅgha of bhikkhus to my hands.”
dhpak1.13:27.1: The Teacher, instead of consenting to the arrangement suggested by Devadatta, refused his request and called him a lick-spittle.
dhpak1.13:27.2: Therefore Devadatta was highly indignant, and now for the first time conceiving hatred towards the Teacher, departed.
dhpak1.13:27.3: The Teacher had Devadatta suspended at Rājagaha.
dhpak1.13:28.1: Devadatta thought to himself: “Now I have been rejected by the ascetic Gotama; now I will make trouble for him.”
dhpak1.13:28.2: With this thought in mind he approached Ajātasattu and said to him: “Youth, aforetime [28.236] men were long-lived,
dhpak1.13:28.3: but now they are short-lived. This makes it probable that you, being a prince, will die soon. Well then!
dhpak1.13:28.4: You kill your father and become king, and I will kill the Fortunate One and become Buddha.” So when Ajātasattu was
dhpak1.13:28.5: established in his kingdom, Devadatta hired men to kill the Realised One. But the men he hired attained the fruition of
dhpak1.13:29.1: Then Devadatta himself climbed Vulture’s Peak and said to himself: “I alone will deprive the ascetic Gotama of life.”
dhpak1.13:29.2: So saying, he split off a piece of rock and hurled it down. But he succeeded only in drawing the Teacher’s blood.
dhpak1.13:29.3: Failing in this way also to kill him, he next dispatched the elephant Nālāgiri against the Teacher. When the elephant approached,
dhpak1.13:29.4: the Elder Ānanda offered his own life on behalf of the Teacher and stood in the breach. The Teacher subdued the elephant,
dhpak1.13:29.5: and then departed from the city and went to the monastery.
dhpak1.13:30.1: After partaking of the offerings of food brought by countless thousands of lay disciples, he taught in due course to the
dhpak1.13:30.2: residents of Rājagaha, 180 millions in number, and 84,000 living beings had comprehension of the Dhamma. Said the bhikkhus:
dhpak1.13:30.3: “How noble is the venerable Ānanda! When so mighty an elephant approached, he offered his own life {1.141} and stood in
dhpak1.13:30.4: front of the Teacher.” The Teacher, hearing the elder praised in this wise, said: “Bhikkhus, this is not the first time
dhpak1.13:30.5: he has renounced his life for my sake; he did the same thing in a previous state of existence,” and in response to a
dhpak1.13:30.6: request of the bhikkhus he related the Short Birth Story about the Goose, the Long Birth Story about the Goose,
dhpak1.13:30.7: and the Birth Story about the Crab.
dhpak1.13:31.1: Devadatta’s wickedness did not by any means become so notorious from his having compassed the king’s death nor from his
dhpak1.13:31.2: hiring murderers to kill the Realised One nor from his splitting off the piece of rock, as it did from his letting loose
dhpak1.13:31.3: the elephant Nālāgiri. For upon that, the people raised a tumult and said: “Devadatta alone had the king killed and hired
dhpak1.13:31.4: murderers and cast down the rock. But now he has turned the elephant Nālāgiri loose. Behold what manner of wrongdoer the
dhpak1.13:31.5: king has on his hands!” The king then, hearing the words of the populace, caused Devadatta’s five hundred cooking-vessels
dhpak1.13:31.6: to be removed and did not thereafter minister to his wants. Likewise the citizens did not so much as offer food to him
dhpak1.13:31.7: when he came to their houses.
dhpak1.13:32.1: When he had thus lost gains and honor, he determined to live by [28.237] deceit. Therefore he approached the Teacher and
dhpak1.13:32.2: made the five demands. But the Teacher rejected his demands, saying: “Enough, Devadatta! Whoever so desires, let him be a forest hermit.”
dhpak1.13:32.3: – “Friends, whose words are the nobler, the words of the Realised One or the words which I myself have uttered? Very well,
dhpak1.13:32.4: venerable Sir, all their life long bhikkhus should be forest-dwellers, beggars, wearers of rags from a dust-heap,
dhpak1.13:32.5: living at the foot of a tree, eating neither fish nor flesh. Whosoever desires release from suffering, let him come with me.”
dhpak1.13:33.1: Some bhikkhus who had but recently went forth and who possessed little intelligence, hearing his words, said:
dhpak1.13:33.2: “Devadatta spoke fair; let us join him.” So they joined him. Thus Devadatta with his five hundred bhikkhus sought to
dhpak1.13:33.3: persuade all manner of people, both hardened and believing, to accept the five points. And living by soliciting food from
dhpak1.13:33.4: various families, he strove to create a schism in the Saṅgha.
dhpak1.13:34.1: The Fortunate One asked him: “Devadatta, is it true, as men say, that you are striving to create schism in the Saṅgha?”
dhpak1.13:34.2: – “It is true,” replied Devadatta. The Teacher said: “Devadatta, it is a grievous thing to create a schism in the Saṅgha.”
dhpak1.13:34.3: Continuing, the Teacher admonished him at length. But Devadatta paid no attention to the Teacher’s words.
dhpak1.13:35.1: He went forth, and seeing the venerable Elder Ānanda going his rounds for alms in Rājagaha, said to him: “Friend Ānanda,
dhpak1.13:35.2: from this day forth I shall keep Observance Day and do Formal Acts of the Saṅgha apart from the Fortunate One.”
dhpak1.13:35.3: The elder told the Fortunate One. When the Teacher realized the fact, he was filled with righteous indignation and said to himself:
dhpak1.13:35.4: “Devadatta is doing that which will be of no profit to him in the worlds of the Devas and the world of humans;
dhpak1.13:35.5: that which will cause him to be tormented in the Avīci hell.” And he reflected:
dhpak1.13:36.1: Dhp 163: Easily done are things not good, unbeneficial for oneself, but that which is beneficial is exceedingly hard to do.
dhpak1.13:37.1: Having pronounced this verse, he then breathed forth the following exalted utterance:
dhpak1.13:38.1: Done with ease by the good is good, good by the bad is done only with great difficulty; bad by the bad is done with ease,
dhpak1.13:38.2: bad by the Noble Ones is done only with great difficulty.
dhpak1.13:39.1: On the Observance Day, as Devadatta sat on one side with his own retinue, he said: “Let whoever approves of these five points take a ticket.”
dhpak1.13:40.1: Five hundred Licchavi princes, novices having little gratitude, took tickets. Devadatta took these bhikkhus with him and went to Gayāsīsa.
dhpak1.13:40.2: When the Teacher heard that he had gone there, he sent forth the two Chief Disciples to bring those bhikkhus back.
dhpak1.13:40.3: The Chief Disciples went there, instructed the bhikkhus by performing miracles and wonders, caused them to drink the Deathless,
dhpak1.13:40.4: and returned through the air, bringing them with them.
dhpak1.13:41.1: Tearing the Fabric Said Kokālika: “Rise, brother Devadatta; Sāriputta and Moggallāna have carried off your bhikkhus.
dhpak1.13:41.2: Do you not remember my saying to you: ‘Friend, trust not Sāriputta and Moggallāna?’” Said Devadatta:
dhpak1.13:41.3: “Sāriputta and Moggallāna cherish wicked desires, are under the control of wicked desires.” As he spoke thus,
dhpak1.13:41.4: he struck the center of his heart with his knee, and straightaway hot blood burst forth from his mouth.
dhpak1.13:42.1: The Return When the bhikkhus saw venerable Sāriputta, surrounded by his retinue of bhikkhus, soaring through the air, they said:
dhpak1.13:42.2: “Venerable Sir, when venerable Sāriputta went hence, he went with but single companion; but now he is returning resplendent
dhpak1.13:42.3: with a great retinue.” The Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, it is not the first time this has happened; when my son was reborn in
dhpak1.13:42.4: the form of an animal, then also did he return to me resplendent.” So saying, he recited the Birth Story about (the Deer Named) Lakkhaṇa:
dhpak1.13:43.1: In the past in the city of Rājagaha in the kingdom of Magadha there ruled a certain king of Magadha, in whose days the
dhpak1.13:43.2: Bodhisatta came to life as a stag. Growing up, he dwelt in the forest as the leader of a herd of a thousand deer.
dhpak1.13:43.3: He had two young ones named Lakkhaṇa (Lucky) and Kāḷa (Unlucky). When he grew old, he handed his charge over to his two sons,
dhpak1.13:43.4: placing five hundred deer under the care of each of them. And so now these two young stags were in charge of the herd.
dhpak1.13:44.1: Towards harvest-time in Magadha, when the crops stand thick in the fields, it is dangerous for the deer in the forests round.
dhpak1.13:44.2: Anxious to kill the creatures that devour their crops, the peasants dig pitfalls, fix stakes, set stone-traps,
dhpak1.13:44.3: and plant snares and other traps; so that many deer are slain.
dhpak1.13:45.1: Accordingly, when the Bodhisatta marked that it was crop-time, he sent for his two sons and said to them: “My children,
dhpak1.13:45.2: it is now the time when crops stand thick in the fields, and many deer meet their death at this season.
dhpak1.13:45.3: We who are old will make shift to stay in one spot; but you will retire each with your herd to the mountainous tracts in
dhpak1.13:45.4: the forest and come back when the crops have been carried.” – “Very good,” said his two sons, and departed with their herds,
dhpak1.13:46.1: Now the men who live along the route, know quite well the times at which deer take to the hills and return thence.
dhpak1.13:46.2: And lying in wait in hiding-places here and there along the route, they shoot and kill numbers of them. The dullard Kāḷa,
dhpak1.13:46.3: ignorant of the times to travel and the times to halt, kept his deer on the march early and late, both at dawn and in the evening,
dhpak1.13:46.4: approaching the very confines of the villages. And the peasants, in ambush or in the open, destroyed numbers of his herd.
dhpak1.13:46.5: Having thus by his crass folly worked the destruction of all these, it was with a very few survivors that he reached the forest.
dhpak1.13:47.1: Lakkhaṇa on the other hand, being wise and astute and having skill in means, never so much as approached the confines of a village.
dhpak1.13:47.2: He did not travel by day, or even in the dawn or evening. Only in the dead of night did he move; and the result was that
dhpak1.13:47.3: he reached the forest without losing a single head of his deer.
dhpak1.13:48.1: Four months they stayed in the forest, not leaving the hills till the crops were carried. On the homeward way Kāḷa,
dhpak1.13:48.2: by repeating his former folly, lost the rest of his herd and returned solitary and alone; whereas Lakkhaṇa had not lost
dhpak1.13:48.3: one of his herd, but had brought back the whole five hundred deer, when he appeared before his parents.
dhpak1.13:48.4: As he saw his two sons returning, the Bodhisatta framed this verse in concert with the herd of deer:
dhpak1.13:49.1: The virtuous one will prosper, he whose way of life is friendly, look at Lakkhaṇa approaching, surrounded by his relatives,
dhpak1.13:49.2: then look at this Kāḷa, who has completely lost his relatives.
dhpak1.13:50.1: The bhikkhus said again: “Venerable Sir, they say that Devadatta seats a Chief Disciple on either side of him and imitates you,
dhpak1.13:50.2: saying: ‘I will teach the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha.’” The Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, this is not the first time he has so done;
dhpak1.13:50.3: in a previous state of existence also he strove to imitate me, but was not able to do so. Supplying the rest of the story,
dhpak1.13:50.4: the Teacher related the Birth Story about (the Hero Crow) Vīrika.
dhpak1.13:51.1: In the past, while Brahmadatta reigned as king in Benares, the Bodhisatta became a cormorant, and dwelt by a certain pool. His name was Vīraka (Hero).
dhpak1.13:52.1: There arose a famine in Kāsi. Men could not spare food for the crows, nor make offerings to Yakkhas and Nāgas.
dhpak1.13:52.2: One by one the crows left the famine-stricken land, and went to the woods.
dhpak1.13:53.1: A certain crow named Saviṭṭhaka, who lived at Benares, took with him his lady crow and went to the place where Vīraka lived,
dhpak1.13:53.2: making his abode beside the same pool.
dhpak1.13:54.1: One day, this crow was seeking food about the pool. He saw how Vīraka went down into it, and made a meal off some fish;
dhpak1.13:54.2: and afterwards came up out of the water again, and stood drying his feathers. “Under the wing of that crow,” he thought,
dhpak1.13:54.3: “plenty of fish are to be got. I will become his servant.” So he drew near.
dhpak1.13:55.1: “What is it, sir?” asked Vīraka. “I want to be your servant, my lord!” was the reply.
dhpak1.13:56.1: Vīraka agreed, and from that time the other served him. And from that time, Vīraka used to eat enough fish to keep him alive,
dhpak1.13:56.2: and the rest he gave to Saviṭṭhaka as soon as he had caught them; and when Saviṭṭhaka had eaten enough to keep him alive,
dhpak1.13:56.3: he gave what was over to his wife.
dhpak1.13:57.1: After a while pride came into his heart. “This crow,” said he, “is black, and so am I: in eyes and beak and feet, too,
dhpak1.13:57.2: there is no difference between us. I don’t want his fish; I will catch my own!” So he told Vīraka that for the future he
dhpak1.13:57.3: intended to go down to the water and catch fish himself. Then Vīraka said: “Good friend, you do not belong to a tribe of
dhpak1.13:57.4: such crows as are born to go into water and catch fish. Don’t destroy yourself!”
dhpak1.13:58.1: But in spite of this attempt to dissuade him, Saviṭṭhaka did not take the warning to heart. Down he went to the pool,
dhpak1.13:58.2: down into the water; but he could not make his way through the weeds and come out again – there he was, entangled in the weeds,
dhpak1.13:58.3: with only the tip of his beak appearing above the water. So not being able to breathe he perished there beneath the water.
dhpak1.13:59.1: The Folly His mate noticed that he did not return, and went to Vīraka to ask news of him. “My lord,” she asked,
dhpak1.13:59.2: “Saviṭṭhaka is not to be seen, where is he?” And as she asked him this, she repeated the first verse:
dhpak1.13:60.1: Have you seen, O Vīraka, the bird having a very sweet voice, with a neck looking like a peacock’s, my husband Saviṭṭhaka?
dhpak1.13:61.1: When Vīraka heard it, he replied, “Yes, I know where he is gone,” and recited the second verse:
dhpak1.13:62.1: That bird at home in water and on land, who constantly enjoys fresh fish to eat: through imitating him Saviṭṭhaka has died,
dhpak1.13:62.2: caught up amongst the lakeside weeds.
dhpak1.13:63.1: On succeeding days, with reference to the same subject, the Teacher related the Birth Story about (the Woodpecker) Kandagalaka
dhpak1.13:64.1: In the past, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, the Bodhisatta entered into life as a woodpecker.
dhpak1.13:64.2: In a wood of acacia trees he lived, and his name was Khadiravaniya, the bird of the acacia wood. He had a comrade named Kandagalaka,
dhpak1.13:64.3: who got his food in a wood full of good fruit.
dhpak1.13:65.1: One day the friend went to visit Khadiravaniya. “My friend is come!” thought Khadiravaniya; and he led him into the acacia wood,
dhpak1.13:65.2: and pecked at the tree-trunks until the insects came out, which he gave to his friend. As each was given him,
dhpak1.13:65.3: the friend pecked it up, and ate it, as if it were a honey cake. As he ate, pride arose in his heart. “This bird is a woodpecker,”
dhpak1.13:65.4: he thought, “and so am I. What need for me to be fed by him? I will get my own food in this acacia wood!”
dhpak1.13:66.1: So he said to Khadiravaniya: “Friend, don’t trouble yourself – I will get my own food in the acacia wood.” Then said the other,
dhpak1.13:66.2: “You belong to a tribe of birds which finds its food in a forest of pithless silk-cotton trees, and trees that bear abundant fruit;
dhpak1.13:66.3: but the acacia is full of pith, and hard. Please do not do so!”
dhpak1.13:67.1: “What!” said Kandagalaka – am I not a woodpecker?” And he would not listen, but pecked at an acacia trunk.
dhpak1.13:67.2: In a moment his beak snapped off, and his eyes bade fair to fall out of his head, and his head split.
dhpak1.13:67.3: So not being able to hold fast to the tree, he fell to the ground, repeating the first verse:
dhpak1.13:68.1: Dear, what is that tree’s name, with sweaty leaves and thorns, where, with just one blow, my cranium has been split?
dhpak1.13:69.1: Having heard this, Khadiravaniya recited the second verse:
dhpak1.13:70.1: Roaming around this, striking in the woods on the pithless branches of useless trees, then hitting a pithy acacia tree,
dhpak1.13:70.2: where the pecker shattered his cranium.
dhpak1.13:71.1: and the Birth Story about Shining Forth: [28.239]
dhpak1.13:72.1: In the past when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a maned lion and dwelt at Gold Den in the Himālayas.
dhpak1.13:72.2: Bounding forth one day from his lair, he looked north and west, south and east, and roared aloud as he went in quest of prey.
dhpak1.13:72.3: Slaying a large buffalo, he devoured the prime of the carcass, after which he went down to a pool, and having drunk his
dhpak1.13:72.4: fill of crystal water turned to go towards his den.
dhpak1.13:73.1: Now a hungry jackal, suddenly meeting the lion, and being unable to make his escape, threw himself at the lion’s feet.
dhpak1.13:73.2: Being asked what he wanted, the jackal replied: “Lord, let me be your servant.” – “Very well,” said the lion,
dhpak1.13:73.3: “serve me and you shall feed on prime meat.” So saying, he went with the jackal following to Gold Den.
dhpak1.13:73.4: Thenceforth the lion’s leavings fell to the jackal, and he grew fat.
dhpak1.13:74.1: Lying one day in his den, the lion told the jackal to scan the valleys from the mountain top, to see whether there were
dhpak1.13:74.2: any elephants or horses or buffaloes about, or any other animals of which he, the jackal, was fond. If any such were in sight,
dhpak1.13:74.3: the jackal was to report and say with due obeisance: “Shine forth in your might, Lord.” Then the lion promised to kill and eat,
dhpak1.13:74.4: giving a part to the jackal. So the jackal used to climb the heights, and whenever he espied below beasts to his taste,
dhpak1.13:74.5: he would report it to the lion, and falling at his feet, say: “Shine forth in your might, Lord.” Hereon the lion would
dhpak1.13:74.6: nimbly bound forth and slay the beast, even if it were a rutting elephant, and share the prime of the carcass with the jackal.
dhpak1.13:74.7: Glutted with his meal, the jackal would then retire to his den and sleep.
dhpak1.13:75.1: Now as time went on, the jackal grew bigger and bigger till be grew haughty. “Have not I too four legs?” he asked himself.
dhpak1.13:75.2: “Why am I a pensioner day by day on others’ bounty? Henceforth I will kill elephants and other beasts, for my own eating.
dhpak1.13:75.3: The lion, king of beasts, only kills them because of the formula: ‘Shine forth in your might, Lord.’
dhpak1.13:75.4: I’ll make the lion call out to me, ‘Shine forth in your might, jackal,’ and then I’ll kill an elephant for myself.”
dhpak1.13:76.1: Accordingly he went to the lion, and pointing out that he had long lived on what the lion had killed, told his desire to
dhpak1.13:76.2: eat an elephant of his own killing, ending with a request to the lion to let him, the jackal, couch in the lion’s corner
dhpak1.13:76.3: in Gold Den while the lion was to climb the mountain to look out for an elephant. The quarry found, he asked that the lion
dhpak1.13:76.4: should come to him in the den and say: ‘Shine forth in [1.307] your might, jackal.’ He begged the lion not to grudge him this much.
dhpak1.13:77.1: Said the lion, “Jackal, only lions can kill elephants, nor has the world ever seen a jackal able to cope with them.
dhpak1.13:77.2: Give up this fancy, and continue to feed on what I kill.” But say what the lion could, the jackal would not give way,
dhpak1.13:77.3: and still pressed his request. So at last the lion gave way, and bidding the jackal couch in the den, climbed the peak
dhpak1.13:77.4: and thence espied an elephant in rut. Returning to the mouth of the cave, he said: “Shine forth in your might, jackal.”
dhpak1.13:77.5: Then from Gold Den the jackal nimbly bounded forth, looked around him on all four sides, and, thrice raising its howl,
dhpak1.13:77.6: sprang at the elephant, meaning to fasten on its head. But missing his aim, he alighted at the elephant’s feet.
dhpak1.13:77.7: The infuriated brute raised its right foot and crushed the jackal’s head, trampling the bones into powder.
dhpak1.13:77.8: Then pounding the carcass into a mass, and dunging upon it, the elephant dashed trumpeting into the forest. Seeing all this,
dhpak1.13:77.9: the Bodhisatta observed, “Now shine forth in your might, jackal,” and uttered this verse:
dhpak1.13:78.1: Your brains are split open, and your head is smashed in, all your ribs are broken, today you did shine forth.
dhpak1.13:79.1: Again one day, hearing the remark: “Devadatta was ungrateful,” the Teacher related the Birth Story about the Quick Bird (and a Lion):
dhpak1.13:80.1: In the past when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta came to life as a woodpecker in the Himālayas.
dhpak1.13:81.1: Now a certain lion, while devouring his prey, had a bone stick in his throat. His throat swelled up so that he could not
dhpak1.13:81.2: take any food and severe pains set in. Then this woodpecker, while intent on seeking its own food, as it was perched on a bough,
dhpak1.13:81.3: saw the lion and asked him, saying: “Friend, what ails you?” He told him what was the matter, and the bird said:
dhpak1.13:81.4: “I would take the bone out of your throat, friend, but I dare not put my head into your mouth, for fear you should eat me up.”
dhpak1.13:81.5: – “Do not be afraid, friend; I will not eat you up. Only save my life.”
dhpak1.13:82.1: “All right,” said the bird, and ordered the lion to lie down upon his side. Then it thought: “Who knows what this fellow will be about?”
dhpak1.13:82.2: And to prevent his closing his mouth, it fixed a stick between his upper and lower jaw, and then putting its head into
dhpak1.13:82.3: the lion’s mouth, it struck the end of the bone with its beak. The bone fell out and disappeared. And then the woodpecker
dhpak1.13:82.4: drew out its head from the lion’s mouth, and with a blow from its beak knocked out the stick, and hopping off sat on the top of a bough.
dhpak1.13:83.1: The lion recovered from his sickness, and one day was devouring a wild buffalo which he had killed. Thought the woodpecker:
dhpak1.13:83.2: “I will now put him to the test,” and perching on a bough above the lion’s head, it fell to conversing with him and uttered the first verse:
dhpak1.13:84.1: We have done our duty to you, with whatever strength we had, King of beasts we revere you, may we receive something from you?
dhpak1.13:85.1: On hearing this the lion repeated the second verse:
dhpak1.13:86.1: I am one who feeds on blood, I am forever cruel, I hold you between my teeth, it is much that you still live.
dhpak1.13:87.1: Again with reference to Devadatta’s going about for the purpose of slaying, he related the Birth Story about the Antelope:
dhpak1.13:88.1: In the past when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta came to life as an antelope, and used to live on fruits in his haunts in the forest.
dhpak1.13:89.1: At one period he was subsisting on the fruit of a Sepaṇṇi tree. And there was a village hunter, whose method was to build
dhpak1.13:89.2: a platform in trees at the foot of which he found the track of deer, and to watch aloft for their coming to eat the fruits of the trees.
dhpak1.13:89.3: When the deer came, he brought them down with a javelin, and sold the flesh for a living.
dhpak1.13:90.1: This hunter one day marked the tracks of the Bodhisatta at the foot of the tree, and made himself a platform up in the boughs.
dhpak1.13:90.2: Having breakfasted early, he went with his javelin into the forest and seated himself on his platform. The Bodhisatta,
dhpak1.13:90.3: too, came abroad early to eat the fruit of that tree; but he was not in too great a hurry to approach it. “For,”
dhpak1.13:90.4: thought he to himself, “sometimes these platform-building hunters build themselves platforms in the boughs.
dhpak1.13:90.5: Can it be that this can have happened here?” And he halted some way off to reconnoitre.
dhpak1.13:91.1: Finding that the Bodhisatta did not approach, the hunter, still seated aloft on his platform, threw fruit down in front of the antelope.
dhpak1.13:91.2: Said the latter to himself: “Here’s the fruit coming to meet me; I wonder if there is a hunter up there.” So he looked,
dhpak1.13:91.3: and looked, till he caught sight of the hunter in the tree; but, feigning not to have seen the man, he shouted:
dhpak1.13:91.4: “My worthy tree, hitherto you have been in the habit of letting your fruit fall straight to the ground like a pendant creeper;
dhpak1.13:91.5: but today you have ceased to act like a tree. And therefore, as you have ceased to behave as becomes a tree, I too must change,
dhpak1.13:91.6: and look for food beneath another tree.” And so saying, he repeated this verse:
dhpak1.13:92.1: For the antelope knows who it is drops fruit from the Sepaṇṇi, I will go to another Sepaṇṇi, I do not like your fruit.
dhpak1.13:93.1: Again when the discussion took this turn: “Devadatta fell away both from gain and honor and from the ascetic life,”
dhpak1.13:93.2: the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, this is not the first time he has so fallen away; in a previous state of existence also he fell away.”
dhpak1.13:93.3: So saying, he related the Birth Story about Falling Both Ways:
dhpak1.13:94.1: In the past when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a Tree Devatā, and there was a certain
dhpak1.13:94.2: village where fishermen dwelt in those days. And one of these fishermen taking his tackle went off with his little boy,
dhpak1.13:94.3: and cast his hook into the most likely waters known to his fellow-fishermen. Now a snag caught his hook and the fisherman
dhpak1.13:94.4: could not pull it up. “What a fine fish!” thought he. “I’d better send my boy off home to my wife and tell her to get up
dhpak1.13:94.5: a quarrel and keep the others at home, so that there’ll be none to want to go shares in my prize.”
dhpak1.13:95.1: Accordingly he told the lad to run off home and tell his mother what a big fish he had hooked and how she was to engage
dhpak1.13:95.2: the neighbours’ attention. Then, fearing his line might break, he flung off his coat and dashed into the water to secure his prize.
dhpak1.13:95.3: But as he groped about for the fish, he struck against the snag and put out both his eyes. Moreover a robber stole his clothes from the bank.
dhpak1.13:95.4: In an agony of pain, with his hands pressed to his blinded eyes, he clambered out trembling in every limb and tried to find his clothes.
dhpak1.13:96.1: Meantime his wife, to occupy the neighbours by a quarrel on purpose, had tricked herself out with a palm-leaf behind one ear,
dhpak1.13:96.2: and had blacked one eye with soot from the saucepan. In this guise, nursing a dog, she came out to call on her neighbours.
dhpak1.13:96.3: “Bless me, you’ve gone mad,” said one woman to her. “Not mad at all,” retorted the fisherman’s wife, “you abuse me without
dhpak1.13:96.4: cause with your slanderous tongue. Come your ways with me to
dhpak1.13:96.5: the village headman and I’ll have you fined eight pieces for slander.”
dhpak1.13:97.1: So with angry words they went off to the village headman. But when the matter was gone into, it was the fisherman’s wife who was fined;
dhpak1.13:97.2: and she was tied up and beaten to make her pay the fine. Now when the Tree Devatā saw how misfortune had befallen both
dhpak1.13:97.3: the wife in the village and the husband in the forest, he stood in the fork of his tree and exclaimed, “Ah, fisherman,
dhpak1.13:97.4: both in the water and on land your labour is in vain, and twofold is your failure.” So saying he uttered this verse:
dhpak1.13:98.1: Eyes are blinded, and clothes are lost, accusations in a friend’s house, both of their doings are wicked, in the water and on dry land.
dhpak1.13:99.1: In this wise did the Teacher, while he was in residence at Rājagaha, relate many Birth Stories about Devadatta.
dhpak1.13:99.2: From Rājagaha he went to Sāvatthī, and took up his residence at Jetavana monastery.
dhpak1.13:100.1: Devadatta’s sickness continued for nine months; at the last, desiring to see the Teacher, he said to his own disciples:
dhpak1.13:100.2: “I desire to see the Teacher; make it possible for me to see him.” They replied: “When you enjoyed good health,
dhpak1.13:100.3: you walked at enmity with the Teacher; we will not lead you to him.” Said Devadatta: “Do not destroy me;
dhpak1.13:100.4: I did indeed conceive hatred towards the Teacher, but the Teacher has not cherished so much as the tip of a hair’s hatred towards me.”
dhpak1.13:101.1: Towards the murderer Devadatta, towards the robber Aṅgulimāla, towards Dhanapāla and Rāhula, towards all he had an even temper. [28.240]
dhpak1.13:102.1: “Let me see the Fortunate One,” begged Devadatta again and again; so finally they laid him on a litter and started out with him.
dhpak1.13:102.2: When the bhikkhus heard that Devadatta was approaching, they informed the Teacher of the fact, saying: “Venerable Sir,
dhpak1.13:102.3: we hear that Devadatta is coming to see you.” – “Bhikkhus, he will not succeed in seeing me in this present existence.”
dhpak1.13:102.4: It is said that from the moment bhikkhus make the five demands, they invariably fail to see the Buddhas again.
dhpak1.13:103.1: “Venerable Sir, he has reached such and such a place; he has reached such and such a place.” – “Let him do as he likes;
dhpak1.13:103.2: he will never succeed in seeing me again.” – “Venerable Sir, now he is only a league distant, now he is only half a league distant,
dhpak1.13:103.3: now he is only a few hundred metres distant, now he has reached the lotus-tank.” – “Even if he enters within the Jetavana,
dhpak1.13:103.4: he will not succeed in seeing me.”
dhpak1.13:104.1: The Earth Those who came with Devadatta set the litter down on the bank of the lotus-tank at the Jetavana and descended
dhpak1.13:104.2: into the tank to bathe. Devadatta arose from his litter and sat down, resting both feet on the ground, whereupon his feet
dhpak1.13:104.3: sank into the earth. By degrees he sank into the earth, first to the ankles, then to the knees, then to the hips,
dhpak1.13:104.4: then to the breast, then to the neck. Finally, when his jaw-bone rested on the ground, he pronounced the following verse:
dhpak1.13:105.1: With these bones, with my breath, I go for refuge to the Buddha, to the greatest amongst humans, to the Deva over Devas,
dhpak1.13:105.2: the guide for those who need taming, to the one with vision all round, to the one with a hundred marks.
dhpak1.13:106.1: There is a tradition that when the Realised One saw that matters had gone thus far, he made a bhikkhu of Devadatta.
dhpak1.13:106.2: And this he did because he became aware of the following: “If he shall remain a lay disciple and not be given the going
dhpak1.13:106.3: forth as a bhikkhu, inasmuch as he has been guilty of grievous crimes, it will be impossible for him to look forwards with
dhpak1.13:106.4: confidence to future existence; but if he shall go forth, no matter how grievous the crimes he has committed,
dhpak1.13:106.5: it will be possible for him to look forwards with confidence to future existence.” {1.148} At the end of 100,000 aeons of
dhpak1.13:106.6: time he will become a Paccekabuddha named Aṭṭhissara.
dhpak1.13:107.1: When Devadatta had sunk into the earth, he was reborn in the Avīci hell. “Since he wronged an unchanging Buddha,
dhpak1.13:107.2: let him endure torture unrelenting,” and such was the torture he suffered. When he had entered the Avīci hell,
dhpak1.13:107.3: which is a hundred leagues in extent, his body became a hundred leagues in height. His head, as far as the outer ear,
dhpak1.13:107.4: entered an iron skull; his feet, as far as the ankles, [28.241] entered earth of iron. An iron stake as thick as the trunk
dhpak1.13:107.5: of a palmyra tree proceeded forth from the west wall of the iron shell, pierced the small of his back, came forth from his breast,
dhpak1.13:107.6: and penetrated the east wall. Another iron stake proceeded forth from the south wall, pierced his right side,
dhpak1.13:107.7: came forth from his left side, and penetrated the north wall. Another iron stake proceeded forth from the top of the iron skull,
dhpak1.13:107.8: pierced his skull, came forth from his lower parts, and penetrated earth of iron. In this position, immovable,
dhpak1.13:107.9: he suffers this mode of torture.
dhpak1.13:108.1: The bhikkhus began a discussion, saying: “All this distance Devadatta came, but failed to see the Teacher,
dhpak1.13:108.2: and was swallowed up by the earth.” The Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, this was not the first time Devadatta wronged me and was
dhpak1.13:108.3: swallowed up by the earth; in a previous state of existence also he was swallowed up by the earth.”
dhpak1.13:109.1: And by way of illustrating the point, he told the story of an incident in his own previous existence as a king of the elephants.
dhpak1.13:109.2: He directed aright a man who had lost his way, allowed him to mount his own back, and carried him to a place of safety,
dhpak1.13:109.3: only to have the man return to him three successive times and saw off first the tips of his tusks, then the middle,
dhpak1.13:109.4: and then the roots. As the man passed out of sight of the Great Being, he was swallowed up by the earth.
dhpak1.13:109.5: {1.149} The Teacher then completed the Sīlavanāga Birth Story:
dhpak1.13:110.1: The ungrateful person, always looking out for an opening, even if given the whole world, still would never be satisfied.
dhpak1.13:111.1: The discussion reverting to the same subject again and again, in order to illustrate the swallowing up of Devadatta by
dhpak1.13:111.2: the earth in his existence as Kalāburājā for an offense against himself in his existence as Khantivādi, he related the
dhpak1.13:111.3: Birth Story about the One who Spoke of Forbearance.
dhpak1.13:112.1: Again, in order to illustrate the swallowing up of Devadatta by the earth in his existence as Mahāpatāparājā for an offense
dhpak1.13:112.2: against himself in his existence as Culla Dhammapāla, he related the Short Birth Story about (Prince) Dhammapāla.
dhpak1.13:113.1: Now when Devadatta was swallowed up by the earth, the populace was pleased and delighted, and raising flags and banners
dhpak1.13:113.2: and plantain trees and setting up brimming jars, held high festival, saying: “His death is indeed our great gain.”
dhpak1.13:114.1: When the bhikkhus reported this incident to the Fortunate One, the Fortunate One said: “Bhikkhus, this is not the first
dhpak1.13:114.2: time the populace has rejoiced at Devadatta’s death; [28.242] in times past also the populace rejoiced thereat.”
dhpak1.13:114.3: And when he had thus spoken, to illustrate the rejoicing of the populace at the death of King Piṅgala of Bārāṇasī,
dhpak1.13:114.4: a man who was hated by all the people for his harshness and cruelty, he related the Birth Story about (the Unjust King) Mahā Piṅgala:
dhpak1.13:115.1: In the past a wicked and unjust king named Mahāpiṅgala reigned at Benares, the tawny king, who did sinfully after his own will and pleasure.
dhpak1.13:115.2: With taxes and fines, and many mutilations and robberies, he crushed the folk as it were sugar-cane in a mill;
dhpak1.13:115.3: he was cruel, fierce, ferocious. For other people he had not a grain of pity; at home he was harsh and implacable towards his wives,
dhpak1.13:115.4: his sons and daughters, to his brahmin courtiers and the householders of the country. He was like a speck of dust that
dhpak1.13:115.5: falls in the eye, like gravel in the broth, like a thorn sticking in the heel.
dhpak1.13:116.1: Now the Bodhisatta was a son of king Mahā Piṅgala. After this king had reigned for a long time, he died.
dhpak1.13:116.2: When he died all the citizens of Benares were overjoyed and laughed a great laugh; they burnt his body with a thousand
dhpak1.13:116.3: cartloads of logs, and quenched the place of burning with thousands of jars of water, and consecrated the Bodhisatta to be king:
dhpak1.13:116.4: they caused a drum of rejoicing to beat about the streets, for joy that they had got them a righteous king.
dhpak1.13:116.5: They raised flags and banners, and decked out the city; at every door was set a pavilion, and scattering parched corn and flowers,
dhpak1.13:116.6: they sat them down upon the decorated platforms under fine canopies, and did eat and drink. The Bodhisatta himself sat
dhpak1.13:116.7: upon a fine divan on a great raised dais, in great magnificence, with a white parasol stretched above him.
dhpak1.13:116.8: The courtiers and householders, the citizens and the doorkeepers stood around their king.
dhpak1.13:117.1: But one doorkeeper, standing not far from the king, was sighing and sobbing. “Good Porter,” said the Bodhisatta, observing him,
dhpak1.13:117.2: “all the people are making merry for joy that my father is dead, but you stand weeping. Come, was my father good and kind to you?”
dhpak1.13:117.3: And with the question he uttered the first verse:
dhpak1.13:118.1: All people were harassed by Piṅgala, now, because he is dead, they feel delight, what was the one with tawny eyes to you?
dhpak1.13:118.2: Why are you crying, watchman of the door?
dhpak1.13:119.1: The man heard, and answered: “I am not weeping for sorrow that Piṅgala is dead. My head would be glad enough.
dhpak1.13:119.2: For king Piṅgala, every time he came down from the palace, or went up into it, would give me eight blows over the head with his fist,
dhpak1.13:119.3: like the blows of a blacksmith’s hammer. So when he goes down to the other world, he will deal eight blows on the head of Yama,
dhpak1.13:119.4: the gatekeeper of hell, as though he were striking me. Then the people there will cry: ‘He is too cruel for us!’
dhpak1.13:119.5: And will send him up again. And I fear he will come and deal fisticuffs on my head again, and that is why I weep.”
dhpak1.13:119.6: To explain the matter he uttered the second verse:
dhpak1.13:120.1: The one with tawny eyes wasn’t dear to me, but his coming back I truly do fear, going from here should he harass Death’s King,
dhpak1.13:120.2: being harassed, he may send him back here.
dhpak1.13:121.1: Finally the bhikkhus asked the Teacher: “Now, venerable Sir, tell us where Devadatta was reborn.” – “Bhikkhus, he was reborn in Avīci.”
dhpak1.13:121.2: – “Venerable Sir, during his life here on earth he suffered, and when he went hence he was reborn in a place of suffering.”
dhpak1.13:121.3: – “Yes, bhikkhus, they that abide in heedlessness, be they bhikkhus or laymen, suffer in both places.” So saying,
dhpak1.13:122.1: 17. Idha tappati, pecca tappati, pāpakārī ubhayattha tappati, “Pāpaṁ mĕ katan”-ti tappati, bhiyyo tappati duggatiṁ gato.
dhpak1.13:123.1: Here he suffers, after death he suffers, the wicked one suffers in both places, he suffers, thinking: “I have done evil,”
dhpak1.13:123.2: gone to a bad fate, he suffers much more.
dhpak1.13:124.1: At the conclusion of the verse many became Stream-enterers and so forth, and benefit arose to many people from the teaching.
